question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,i+j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2t)-{1}^{2})\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
